advisor.summary: Sections 274(j) and 74(c) together preserve one of the few remaining clean double benefits in compensation: a qualifying employee achievement award is deductible to the employer and excluded from the employee's income, and §3121(a)(20) keeps it out of FICA wages on both sides. The qualification rules are narrow and mechanical — tangible personal property only, awarded for length of service or safety achievement as part of a meaningful presentation, capped at $400 per employee per year without a plan and $1,600 under a written qualified plan. The dollars are deliberately small; the value is converting recognition spending the client already does into a channel that beats a taxable bonus dollar for dollar and survives a payroll exam.
mechanics: §274(j)(3)(A) defines the award: an item of tangible personal property, given for length of service or safety achievement, as part of a meaningful presentation, and not disguised compensation; the TCJA wrote the exclusions into the statute — cash, gift cards and certificates, vacations, meals, lodging, tickets, and securities never qualify.

The deduction and matching exclusion cap at $400 per employee per year for nonqualified awards, and $1,600 in aggregate where awards are made under a written qualified plan that does not favor highly compensated employees and holds average award cost to $400 or less.

Length-of-service awards fail inside the employee's first five years and cannot repeat for the same employee more often than every five years under §274(j)(4)(B); safety awards fail if made to managers, administrators, clerical, or other professional employees, or once more than 10 percent of eligible employees receive one in the year.
The employee-side exclusion runs through §74(c) and is limited to the employer's deductible amount — an award over the cap puts the excess, not the whole award, on the W-2.
§3121(a)(20) excludes qualifying awards from FICA wages, completing the result: no income tax, no payroll tax on either side, full deduction.

requirements: W-2 employees and genuine length-of-service or safety milestones to recognize — an owner-only program is not what this rule is for.
Tangible personal property only: a watch, tools, equipment — never cash, gift cards, or broadly redeemable points.
A real presentation moment (recognition event or all-hands), not an item slipped into a paycheck.
For the $1,600 ceiling: a written plan with nondiscriminatory eligibility and a $400-or-less average award cost.
risks: The leading exam theory is reclassification of cash equivalents: gift cards are W-2 wages by statute regardless of amount, and a payroll exam applies the adjustment across every recipient and every open year — there is no de minimis defense once the item is a card.
Awards above the deductible limit push the excess into the employee's income under §74(c) — the clean design stays inside the caps rather than defending overages.
Length-of-service awards given early or too often, and safety awards reaching managers or more than 10 percent of eligible staff, fail by statute with no facts-and-circumstances rescue.
A program aimed mostly at the owner reads as disguised distributions, not employee recognition.
stateNotes: Conformity: states that begin with federal AGI or federal taxable income conform to the §74(c) exclusion automatically — the award never appears in the state base.
PTET interaction: award costs are ordinary entity deductions and already reduce the income a pass-through entity tax election is computed on; no separate PTET step is needed.
Missouri: conforms through its federal starting point (RSMo §143.121) with no addback, so the exclusion and the deduction both carry through to the Missouri return.
reviewChecklist: Every planned award is tangible property — the catalog contains no cash, cards, or certificate-style items.
Milestone timing verified against the five-year rules and the 10 percent safety-award ceiling.
Written plan in place (if the $1,600 limit is used) with eligibility that does not favor highly compensated employees.
Payroll instructed: qualifying awards stay off the W-2, and any non-qualifying gift goes on it.

client.teaser: Reward loyal employees in a way the tax system leaves completely alone.
client.headline: Recognize your team — tax-free for them, deductible for you
plainEnglish: Almost anything you give an employee counts as taxable pay. Bonuses, gift cards, even a holiday certificate all land on the W-2. The tax law keeps one clean exception: real, physical gifts that mark years of service or a safety milestone.

Done right, the business deducts the cost and the employee owes nothing. No income tax and no payroll tax on either side. The gift must be an actual item — a watch, quality tools, good gear. It has to mark a real milestone, like five or ten years with you. And it should be presented at a real moment, like a team lunch.

With a simple written plan, you can give up to $1,600 of value per honoree. A bonus that size would cost you payroll tax and leave the employee maybe $1,100 after withholding. Same generosity, better math, and a better moment.
client.analogy: A gold watch handed over at the company dinner and the same value tucked into a paycheck are worlds apart at tax time. Only one of them is taxed — and it is not the watch.
benefits: Tax-free to the employee — no income tax, no payroll tax
